source.title: Leveraging Large Language Models in Visual Speech Recognition: Model Scaling, Context-Aware Decoding, and Iterative Polishing
source.authors: Zehua Liu; Xiaolou Li; Li Guo; Lantian Li; Dong Wang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a model-size sweep to visual speech recognition and reports downstream recognition results; it does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce the original loss-scaling method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CER for multiple decoder sizes in its scaling test, so those results bear on V6. Results for context-aware decoding, iterative polishing, and their combination are not rows: they test decoding interventions rather than scaling or downstream predictability with scale. The Transformer comparison is not itself a size-scaling result.
record.test_reason: The scaling test compares CER in visual speech recognition across Qwen2.5 decoder sizes (7B, 14B, 32B) with a fixed visual encoder and QLoRA fine-tuning. That bears on V6, downstream performance improving with scale, in a new setting. No pretraining loss is measured and no law is fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim to have "confirmed the existence of the LLM's scaling law in VSR tasks", meaning larger LLM decoders consistently give lower CER. Note that this rests on three sizes with no fitted law, and the 32B-Instruct gain is confounded with instruction tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream character error rate in a visual speech recognition task across decoder sizes; it does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss or fit the original scaling laws.
record.problems: The scaling test reports CER rather than pretraining loss and does not fit a power law or test predictions from smaller runs. It reports one dataset and three sizes for the Qwen2.5 base-model sweep; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on V6 were omitted. Tables 2–4 report context-aware decoding, iterative polishing, and combined decoding interventions rather than a size-scaling comparison.

untested.parts: Whether the improvement is predictable: no curve or power law is fitted, there is no extrapolation, and no link to pretraining loss is tested. Only three sizes, one dataset, single runs, no uncertainty.
Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss form in other modalities or regimes. VSR CER by size is reported, but no loss law.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label (no fitted predictive relationship, few sizes) describes untested parts, not a qualification of V6, so it was dropped and moved to untested. The Transformer baseline and Tables 2–4 (decoding interventions) are correctly excluded. Table 2 shows larger CAD gains for 32B-Instruct than for 7B, but this confounds size with instruction tuning and is not a size-scaling result.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fits and bottleneck conditions.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens across compute budgets.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes; the paper reports VSR recognition performance by decoder size, not a loss law.
The study measures downstream CER across decoder sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship or test prediction from pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5 base decoders 7B→14B→32B, QLoRA fine-tuned for 17k steps on CNVSRC.Single, Valid and Test splits
relationships.reason: CER falls monotonically with decoder size: Valid 46.48→44.30→43.87%, Test 45.20→42.94→42.50% (r1–r3, r5–r7). Gains shrink sharply from 14B to 32B (~0.4 pt versus ~2.2 pt).
relationships.display_finding: Validation CER fell from 46.48% to 44.30% to 43.87% and test CER from 45.20% to 42.94% to 42.50%, with gains shrinking from about 2.2 to 0.4 points.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5 base decoders from 7B to 32B on CNVSRC.Single.Valid and Test
reader_labels.reason: CER decreases as decoder size rises in the reported base-model comparisons (r1–r3 and r5–r7), consistent with downstream performance improving with scale.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports a monotonic size comparison but does not fit or evaluate a quantitative predictive relationship; the sweep covers only the stated decoder sizes and dataset (r1–r8).
